cases.promptMarkdown:
Analyse the CI history below and tell the team which tests are flaky, why, and what to do with each.

Ten CI runs of the e2e suite (120 tests) on the same commit, c0ffee1, on main. Playwright, 4 workers, retries 0. P = passed, F = failed.

| Test | R1 | R2 | R3 | R4 | R5 | R6 | R7 | R8 | R9 | R10 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cart > updates the total when the quantity changes | P | F | P | P | F | P | P | P | F | P |
| profile > saves a new avatar | F | F | F | F | F | F | F | F | F | F |
| search > filters results by tag | P | F | P | F | P | P | F | P | P | F |
| orders > shows the latest order first | P | P | F | P | P | P | P | F | P | P |
| login > signs in with valid credentials | P | P | P | P | P | P | P | P | P | P |

Failure messages (the same message in every failed run of that test):

- cart > updates the total when the quantity changes: Timeout 5000ms exceeded waiting for getByTestId('cart-total') to have text "€58.00". The test clicks "+" and reads the total right after page.waitForTimeout(300).
- profile > saves a new avatar: expect(received).toBe(expected). Expected: "avatar.png". Received: undefined.
- search > filters results by tag: expected 3 results, received 5. Run alone (npx playwright test search.spec.ts --workers=1 --repeat-each=20) it passed 20 of 20. It uses the seeded tag "summer", which tags.spec.ts renames during its own run.
- orders > shows the latest order first: Expected "Order #1043", Received "Order #1042". A --repeat-each=50 run of this spec alone, with web-first assertions and a new user for every run, failed 3 of 50; in those runs GET /orders returned the list without the new order for up to 2 seconds after the order was created.

Where information is missing, state your assumption and continue; do not ask questions. Reply with the deliverable only, as Markdown, starting at its first line, with no introduction and no code fence around it. Do not create or edit files.

## Flaky-test triage for c0ffee1 (10 runs, retries 0)

| Test | Fails | Verdict | Owner action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cart > updates the total when the quantity changes | 3/10 | Flaky, test-side race (app cause possible) | Fix the test now, keep it running |
| profile > saves a new avatar | 10/10 | Not flaky, deterministic failure | Treat as a regression, fix today |
| search > filters results by tag | 4/10 | Flaky, cross-test data pollution | Fix the fixture in both specs, keep it running |
| orders > shows the latest order first | 2/10 | Flaky, real app bug (read-after-write lag) | File a bug, quarantine the test with a ticket |
| login > signs in with valid credentials | 0/10 | Stable | None, use as the control |

Only three of the five are flaky. One is a plain failure that has been mislabelled, and one is the test correctly catching a product bug.

### cart > updates the total when the quantity changes

**What is happening.** The assertion already waits five seconds for the total to read €58.00, so the 300 ms sleep is not what fails. The total never reached the expected value in those five seconds. That leaves two candidate causes. Either the click on "+" is dropped because it lands before the page's handlers are attached, so nothing updates. Or the update is a server round-trip that sometimes exceeds five seconds under four parallel workers. Assumption: the "+" button triggers a request to recalculate the total, and no trace was retained from the failing runs.

**What to do.**
- Delete the `page.waitForTimeout(300)`. It adds nothing and hides intent.
- Before clicking, assert a precondition that proves the page is interactive, such as the quantity reading "1" and the button being enabled.
- After clicking, assert the quantity reads "2" before asserting the total. This splits the two causes: if the quantity never changes, the click was dropped and it is a test bug. If the quantity changes but the total does not, it is an app or performance bug.
- Turn on trace retention for failures in the Playwright config so the next failure shows the request timing.
- Keep the test in the suite. The fix is small and the failure rate is high enough that it will reappear quickly if the diagnosis is wrong.

### profile > saves a new avatar

**What is happening.** It fails ten times out of ten with the same message. That is a deterministic failure, not flakiness. The received value is undefined, which means the field the test reads is missing from the object or response. The most likely causes are a renamed or removed field in the profile API or page model, or a save that silently does nothing. Assumption: this started with c0ffee1 or a recent commit on main, since it is green nowhere.

**What to do.**
- Stop treating this as flaky and remove it from any flaky list. Retries will never make it pass.
- Bisect it against recent main commits and assign it to the owner of the profile feature today. Main is red until it is fixed or the offending change is reverted.
- If the field was intentionally renamed, update the test in the same change that renamed it.

### search > filters results by tag

**What is happening.** Alone it passes 20 of 20. In the suite it fails four of ten, always with extra results. The tests share one seeded database, and tags.spec.ts renames the "summer" tag that search.spec.ts filters on. Whether search fails depends on which worker runs which spec first, which is why the failures look random. This is order-dependent data pollution, not a bug in search.

**What to do.**
- Make tags.spec.ts create its own tag to rename instead of mutating the shared seed. That is the root cause and the primary fix.
- Make search.spec.ts create a uniquely named tag per test, for example suffixed with the test ID, tag a known number of items, and filter on that. Then no other spec can disturb it.
- Do not fix this by running with one worker, by forcing spec order, or by enabling retries. Each of those hides the coupling and slows every run.
- Grep the suite for other tests that mutate seeded rows. The same pattern is likely elsewhere.

### orders > shows the latest order first

**What is happening.** The test is sound. It uses a fresh user per run and web-first assertions, and it still fails three of fifty in isolation. The failing runs show GET /orders omitting the just-created order for up to two seconds. That is a read-after-write consistency gap in the orders service, probably a read replica, a cache, or asynchronous indexing. A retrying assertion cannot help because the page fetches the list once and renders it. A real user who places an order and lands on the list page will sometimes not see it, which is a product bug.

**What to do.**
- File a bug against the orders service with the fifty-run evidence. The fix belongs there: read from the primary after a write, invalidate the cache on create, or return the created order so the UI can merge it.
- Quarantine the test with the ticket number and an expiry date so it stops blocking merges while the bug is open. Keep it running in a non-blocking job so you can see when the fix lands.
- Do not loosen the test by adding a reload loop or a longer timeout unless product explicitly decides that a two-second delay is acceptable behaviour. If they do, encode that decision as a poll that reloads with a documented bound, and say why in the test.

### Suite-wide

- Keep retries at zero. It is the reason these ten runs produced usable data. Turning retries on would have hidden cart, search, and orders and left profile as the only visible failure.
- Add trace retention on failure to the shared Playwright config. Three of the four diagnoses above would have been immediate with a trace.
- Define flaky as a test that both passes and fails on the same commit. Profile does not meet that bar, and orders meets it only because the app is flaky, not the test.
- Re-run the same ten-run check on the fix commit. The target is zero failures on cart and search, profile green, and orders still failing in the non-blocking job until the service fix ships.

# Flaky-test analysis: e2e suite on c0ffee1

**Bottom line.** Three of the five tests are flaky, one is a deterministic failure that is not flaky, and one is healthy. Even with the deterministic failure fixed, only 2 of the 10 runs would have been green. The suite cannot gate merges until the three flaky tests are fixed at the root. Do not turn retries on to hide them.

| Test | Failures | Verdict | Root cause | Owner of the fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cart > updates the total when the quantity changes | 3/10 | Flaky | Fixed sleep plus an unverified click; the click is lost or the update outruns the 5 s expect timeout under load | Test |
| profile > saves a new avatar | 10/10 | Broken, not flaky | Deterministic regression or environment gap | App or test setup |
| search > filters results by tag | 4/10 | Flaky | Shared seed data mutated by another spec running in parallel | Test (tags.spec.ts) |
| orders > shows the latest order first | 2/10, 3/50 alone | Flaky | Backend returns stale order list for up to 2 s after a write | App, with a test-side guard |
| login > signs in with valid credentials | 0/10 | Stable | None | None |

## Assumptions

- Each test gets its own user and cart unless the message says otherwise. All workers share one database and one seed dataset.
- The profile test fails identically on a developer machine. If it passes locally, the cause is environmental rather than a code regression. The actions below cover both cases.
- "Flaky" means the same commit gives different results across runs. A test that fails every time is a bug, not flakiness, and is treated separately.

## 1. cart > updates the total when the quantity changes

**What happens.** Passes 7 of 10. The failing runs all time out waiting for the total to read "€58.00".

**Why.** The test clicks "+", sleeps 300 ms, then asserts the total. The assertion itself retries for 5 s, so the sleep is not the direct cause. The total never reaches the expected value within roughly 5.3 s. Two causes fit a 30 percent failure rate under 4 parallel workers:

- The click fires before the handler is attached. Playwright considers the button actionable once it is visible and enabled, which can be before the framework has hydrated it. The click is swallowed and the total never changes.
- The quantity update round-trips to the server and, under load from the other workers, takes longer than the 5 s expect timeout.

The failure message does not include the received text, so the two cannot be told apart from this evidence alone. If the received text equals the starting total, the click was lost. If it is a different value such as a doubled increment, the click registered twice.

**What to do.**

1. Delete the fixed sleep. Sleeps add time to the fast path and do not help the slow path.
2. Assert the starting state before clicking, for example that the quantity shows 1 and the total shows the pre-click value. This proves the page is ready and makes the failure readable.
3. Make the click observable. Wait for the quantity field to show 2, or wait for the response to the quantity-update request, before asserting the total.
4. Record the received value when it fails. Run the spec alone with a high repeat count, as was done for search and orders, and check whether it still fails. If it only fails in parallel, the cause is server load and the expect timeout for this assertion should be raised to a realistic bound while the slow endpoint is profiled.
5. Until the fix lands, mark it with `test.fixme` so main can go green. Do not delete it.

## 2. profile > saves a new avatar

**What happens.** Fails 10 of 10 with the same assertion: expected "avatar.png", received undefined.

**Why.** This is not flaky. The field the test reads does not exist in the response or the DOM. Likely causes, in order:

- The commit renamed or moved the avatar field, for example from a filename to a URL object, and the test still reads the old path.
- The upload never happens in CI because the fixture file is missing from the checkout or the upload is blocked, so the profile has no avatar.

**What to do.**

1. Run the test on the parent of c0ffee1. If it passes there, this commit broke it and the author should fix the app or update the assertion to the new shape. If it fails there too, it is a CI environment gap. Check that the fixture image is committed and that the path is resolved relative to the spec file, not the working directory.
2. Add an assertion that the upload request returned success before asserting on the saved value, so future failures point at the right layer.
3. Treat this as a blocking failure, not a candidate for quarantine.

## 3. search > filters results by tag

**What happens.** Passes 6 of 10. Fails with "expected 3 results, received 5". Passes 20 of 20 when run alone.

**Why.** Test pollution. The spec filters by the seeded tag "summer". The tags spec renames that same tag during its own run. With 4 workers and no fixed ordering, whether the rename lands before the search assertion is a race. "Received 5" rather than 0 suggests the search either falls back to unfiltered results when the tag is not found, or the tags spec renames a different tag to "summer" and the filter matches extra items. Either way the trigger is the same.

**What to do.**

1. Fix the tags spec, not the search spec. It should create its own tag in a fixture and rename that, leaving the seed data untouched. Tests that mutate shared seed data will keep producing failures like this in other specs.
2. Harden the search spec as well. Create the tag and the three tagged items in a fixture so the test owns every row it depends on.
3. Do not serialize the suite or add a global lock. That hides the dependency and slows every run.
4. Check the fallback behaviour. If filtering by a tag that no longer exists shows all results, that is a product question worth raising, since a user following a stale link would see the same thing.

## 4. orders > shows the latest order first

**What happens.** Fails 2 of 10 in CI and 3 of 50 when run alone with web-first assertions and a fresh user per run. In the failing runs the orders endpoint returned the list without the new order for up to 2 s after creation.

**Why.** The flakiness is in the system under test, not the test. Reading your own write is not guaranteed for up to 2 s. Typical causes are a read replica behind the primary, a cached list response, or an asynchronous projection or index that the list query reads from. The web-first assertion cannot rescue this, because the page fetches the list once on navigation and the stale response is already rendered. Retrying the DOM check does not refetch the data.

**What to do.**

1. Decide whether this is acceptable product behaviour. If the app sends the user to the orders page right after placing an order, real users will hit the same stale list. Treat that as a backend bug: file it, and have the owners either read from the primary after a write, invalidate the cache on create, or return the created order in the response and merge it client side.
2. Guard the test against it in the meantime, without hiding the bug. Poll the orders endpoint with `expect.poll` until the new order appears, then navigate and assert. Keep a separate test, marked as expected to fail against the known bug, that navigates immediately. It will start passing when the backend is fixed and tell you the guard can be removed.
3. Do not add retries or raise the expect timeout for this test. Neither changes what the page fetched.

## 5. login > signs in with valid credentials

Stable across all runs. No action.

## Suite-level actions

- Keep retries at 0 for now. Retries would have turned 8 red runs into mostly green ones while leaving every one of these defects in place. Once the three flaky tests are fixed, set retries to 1 with the flaky-test report enabled so new flakiness is tracked instead of hidden.
- Make the shared-seed rule explicit in the test guidelines. Specs create the data they mutate; seed data is read only.
- Add received values to assertion messages where they are missing, as in the cart test. Two of the four failures here could not be fully diagnosed from CI output alone.
- Re-run the suite 10 times on the same commit after the fixes. The goal is 10 of 10 green with retries at 0.

# Flaky-test analysis: e2e suite on c0ffee1 (10 runs, 4 workers, retries 0)

## Summary

| Test | Pass rate | Verdict | Root cause | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| profile > saves a new avatar | 0/10 | **Broken, not flaky** | Avatar not persisted or not returned (`undefined`) | Fix forward or revert today; main is red |
| search > filters results by tag | 6/10 | **Flaky: test isolation** | tags.spec.ts renames the shared seeded tag "summer" while search.spec.ts runs in a parallel worker | Fix the data coupling in the tests; no quarantine |
| cart > updates the total when the quantity changes | 7/10 | **Flaky: race in the test (probably)** | Fixed `waitForTimeout(300)` plus an assertion that still times out at 5 s; the click or the state is being lost | Rewrite the test; escalate to product bug if quantity itself never updates |
| orders > shows the latest order first | 8/10 CI, 47/50 isolated | **Flaky: product bug (read-after-write)** | `GET /orders` returns stale data for up to 2 s after creation | File a backend bug; make the test tolerate it only as a stopgap |
| login > signs in with valid credentials | 10/10 | Stable | n/a | None, keep as control |

Assumptions used throughout: one shared seeded database across all four workers (not a DB per worker), spec files are scheduled onto workers in a non-deterministic order, and the "received" text for the cart failure was not captured.

## Per-test detail

### profile > saves a new avatar — not flaky, deterministic failure

It fails 10 of 10 with the same message. Flakiness means intermittent; this is a straight failure on this commit. `Received: undefined` means the field the test reads does not exist on the object it reads it from. Two candidates:

- **Product regression in c0ffee1**: the save endpoint stopped returning or storing the avatar filename (e.g. a renamed response field or a dropped column in a serializer).
- **Test bug**: the test reads the wrong property path after a legitimate API shape change.

What to do: treat it as a blocking red build, not a flake. Diff c0ffee1 against the last green commit for the profile save path and the response shape. Do not quarantine; quarantining a 100 % failure hides a regression. If it is a product bug, revert or hotfix. If the API shape changed intentionally, update the test in the same PR that changed the shape.

### search > filters results by tag — flaky, cross-spec data coupling

Passes 20/20 alone with one worker, fails about 40 % in CI with four workers. That pattern is the signature of a shared-state collision, and the mechanism is already identified: tags.spec.ts renames the seeded tag "summer" while search.spec.ts is filtering by it. Whether it fails depends on which spec gets scheduled first, which varies run to run. "Expected 3, received 5" is consistent with the filter matching nothing or a different tag and falling through to a broader result set.

What to do, in priority order:

1. **Give each spec its own data.** Both specs should create their own tag with a unique name (for example `summer-${testInfo.testId}`) in a fixture and delete it in teardown. Neither spec should touch the global seed.
2. **tags.spec.ts is the offender, not search.spec.ts.** A test that mutates shared seed data is a bug regardless of who it breaks. Fix the mutation there even if search is also made self-contained.
3. **Do not** mark search.spec.ts serial or move it to a separate project as the fix. That hides the coupling and will resurface the next time anyone adds a test that uses "summer".
4. Add a lint rule or review checklist item: no spec may rename or delete seeded fixtures.

No quarantine needed; the fix is small and the cause is known.

### cart > updates the total when the quantity changes — flaky, race in the test

Fails 30 %. Note the failure message: "Timeout 5000ms exceeded waiting for getByTestId('cart-total') to have text". That is a web-first assertion that already auto-retries for 5 s. So the 300 ms sleep is a smell, but it is not by itself the reason the test fails; the total never reaches €58.00 in roughly 5.3 s. Something upstream of the assertion is wrong. Most likely explanations:

- **Click is swallowed.** The "+" button is rendered before its handler is attached (hydration or a late-bound listener), so the click lands on a dead element and nothing updates. The 300 ms sleep is a tell that someone saw this before and papered over it.
- **Wrong starting state.** If the cart belongs to a shared seeded user, another worker's test can add or remove items, so the correct total is sometimes not €58.00. This would be the same class of bug as the search failure.
- Least likely: the update genuinely takes more than 5 s under four-worker load.

What to do:

1. Remove `page.waitForTimeout(300)`. Fixed sleeps are never correct in Playwright and this one is masking the real cause.
2. Before clicking, wait for the control to be actionable in a meaningful sense: assert the initial quantity and initial total, then click, then `await expect(quantity).toHaveText('2')` **before** asserting the total. This splits the failure: if the quantity assertion fails, the click was lost and it is a product hydration bug; if the quantity passes and the total fails, it is a pricing or network problem.
3. Capture `trace: 'retain-on-failure'` and the received text; the current report does not say what the total actually showed.
4. Use a per-test cart (fresh user or cleared cart in a fixture) so the expected total does not depend on other workers.

Keep it running while this is done; 30 % is tolerable for a few days with the trace capture turned on because the trace is the diagnostic you need.

### orders > shows the latest order first — flaky, but the bug is in the product

This one is different and the team should not file it with the others. It was already re-run with web-first assertions and a fresh user per run, which eliminates test timing and test isolation, and it still failed 3 of 50 (6 %). The observation is precise: after creating an order, `GET /orders` returns the pre-creation list for up to 2 s. That is a read-after-write consistency gap in the backend. Candidates: reads served from a replica that lags the primary, a response cache or CDN TTL on `GET /orders`, or async indexing between the write store and the read model.

This is user-visible behaviour, not just a test artefact. A real user who places an order and lands on the order list can see it missing for two seconds.

What to do:

1. **File a backend bug** with the 2 s window and the 6 % reproduction rate. The right fix is read-your-writes: route the read after a write to the primary, bypass or invalidate the cache for that user on write, or have the order-creation response return the order and have the UI use that without re-fetching.
2. **Stopgap in the test only if the team accepts the 2 s window as product behaviour.** In that case wrap the read in `await expect(async () => { ... }).toPass({ timeout: 5_000 })` or `expect.poll`, and leave a comment linking the bug so the tolerance is removed once the backend is fixed.
3. Do not quarantine. At 6 % with retries 0 it will keep hurting, but it is a real signal and quarantining it would turn a product bug into noise.

### login > signs in with valid credentials — stable

10/10. No action. Useful as a control: it shows the infrastructure and auth path are healthy, which rules out an environment-wide cause for the others.

## Suite-level recommendations

- **Turn on `retries: 1` in CI** but configure the reporter to flag "flaky" (passed on retry) separately from "passed". Retries should make the build green while fixes land; they should not hide that a test needed retrying. Keep `retries: 0` locally and for the repeat-each investigations.
- **Enable `trace: 'retain-on-failure'`** suite-wide. Two of the four failures could have been diagnosed from the first failing run with a trace.
- **Stop sharing mutable seed data across workers.** Two of the four problem tests trace to shared state or likely do. Either seed per worker (`workerIndex`-scoped data) or make every test create and clean up what it touches.
- **Ban `page.waitForTimeout` by lint.** It appears in the cart test and there are probably others.
- **Separate "always fails" from "sometimes fails" in triage.** profile was listed alongside the flaky tests, but a 0/10 result is a broken build and needs a different response (revert or fix now) from a 70 % test (fix this week).

## cart > updates the total when the quantity changes

**What the data says.** Three failures out of ten, no pattern across runs, identical message every time. The assertion is web-first, so it retried for five seconds and the total never became €58.00. That rules out the assertion being slightly early. The page genuinely did not reach the expected state within five seconds.

**Why.** The test sleeps for a fixed time rather than waiting for a condition, so it carries no information about whether the click took effect. The most likely failure path is that the click landed before the quantity control was interactive, for example before hydration or before the initial cart fetch finished, so the click was dropped and the total stayed at its starting value. A slower CI worker under four-way parallel load makes that window wider, which fits the roughly one in three rate.

**What to do.**
- Fix now rather than quarantine. A test that fails one run in three is the biggest single cause of red pipelines after the profile test.
- Delete the fixed wait. Before clicking, assert the starting state, for example that the total shows the single-item price and the "+" button is enabled. ## profile > saves a new avatar

**What the data says.** Ten failures out of ten with the same message. This is not flaky. It is deterministically broken on this commit.

**Why.** The field the test reads is undefined after the save. Either the upload response or the profile state no longer carries the avatar filename, or the test reads a property that was renamed. Both explanations point to a change that landed on or before c0ffee1.

**What to do.**
- Do not label it flaky and do not quarantine it as a flake. Treating a consistent failure as flaky hides a regression.
- Bisect to the commit that first broke it. If the product changed, fix or revert the product. If the API shape changed intentionally, update the test.

**What the data says.** Four failures out of ten in the parallel suite, zero failures in twenty isolated runs. The failure is two extra results, not a timeout. That combination is the signature of cross-test interference, not timing inside the test.

**Why.** search.spec.ts filters by the seeded tag "summer" and expects three hits. tags.spec.ts renames that same tag as part of its own flow. With four workers the two files sometimes run concurrently or in the wrong order, and whether search sees three or five results depends on which side of the rename it lands on. The test that fails is the victim. The test that causes it is tags.spec.ts.

**What to do.**
- Fix tags.spec.ts first. It should create its own tag to rename and never touch shared seed data. That stops it from polluting any other spec, not just search.

This keeps the test running and keeps it meaningful without being red for a known cause.

Ten passes out of ten. Nothing to do. It is useful as a control showing the environment itself was healthy across all ten runs.

**profile > saves a new avatar is not flaky.** It fails in every run with the same assertion: expected "avatar.png", received undefined. A test that fails deterministically with identical output across ten runs is a broken feature or a broken test, not an intermittent one. Received undefined means the field is missing from the response or page model, so either the save path no longer writes the avatar or the read path no longer returns it. Do not quarantine and do not retry. Find the commit that introduced it by bisecting backwards from c0ffee1, assign it to the owning team, and treat main as broken until it passes. If investigation shows the test is reading a renamed field rather than a real regression, fix the test, but the product should be the first suspect.

The assertion itself has a 5 s window and still timed out, so the total never changed at all, which points to the click being lost rather than the recalculation being slow. The most common reason is clicking a button before its handler is attached while the page is still hydrating, and the sleep is a sign someone already tried to paper over that race. Under four workers CI is slower, so the 300 ms guess fails more often. Remove the fixed sleep. Before clicking, wait on a real readiness signal such as the button being enabled or the initial cart request having completed. After clicking, assert the quantity field first with a web-first assertion, then the total. That split also makes a future failure tell you whether the click or the calculation was lost. npx playwright test cart.spec.ts --workers=4 --repeat-each=50

**search > filters results by tag is test pollution, not a product problem.** It passes 20 of 20 alone and fails only when run alongside the rest of the suite. tags.spec.ts renames the seeded "summer" tag, so the result depends on which worker reaches which spec first. The fact that it returns more results than expected rather than fewer suggests the rename makes extra items match or drops the filter entirely, which is worth a glance but does not change the fix. The fix belongs in both specs. tags.spec.ts should create its own tag and rename that, never a shared seed. search.spec.ts should create its own uniquely named tag and the records that carry it, so it cannot be affected by any other test. Do not fix this by forcing serial execution or dependency ordering, since that hides the coupling and slows the suite. Verify by running both specs together under parallelism:

```
npx playwright test search.spec.ts tags.spec.ts --workers=4 --repeat-each=20
```

**orders > shows the latest order first is a real product bug that the test is catching.** This test is already written the way we want: web-first assertions and a fresh user per run. It still fails alone at a lower rate, and the failing runs show GET /orders omitting an order for up to 2 s after it was created. That is a read-after-write consistency gap, most likely a read replica, a cache, or an asynchronous index. The failure rate roughly triples under four workers, which fits a lag that grows under load. A user who places an order and lands on the orders page would hit the same thing. File a product bug against the orders service and the orders page. The right product fix is either to serve the list from the primary for the creating user immediately after a write or to have the page refetch or optimistically insert the new order. Until that lands, quarantine the test with an annotation that links the ticket so main can be green without losing the record. Do not loosen the assertion or add a longer timeout, because that would hide the bug. If product decides eventual consistency is the intended contract, the page must refetch and the test should poll up to the agreed bound, but that is a product decision to record, not a test shortcut.

**login > signs in with valid credentials is stable.** It passed in all ten runs and nothing needs to change. It is useful as the control that confirms the environment itself was healthy during every run.

## profile > saves a new avatar

**What the data shows.** It failed in every run with the same message. The expected value is the filename and the received value is undefined. There is no variance, so this is not flakiness and should not be labelled or quarantined as such.

**Likely cause.** Undefined rather than a wrong value usually means the property the test reads no longer exists. Either the API response or page object stopped exposing the avatar field, or the upload now completes asynchronously and the test reads before the field is populated. Both would be deterministic.

**Assumption.** I do not have the result for the previous commit. I assume the test passed before c0ffee1 and this is a regression introduced by the commit or by an environment change that landed with it.

**Action.** Bisect against the previous green commit. If the product changed, it is a blocking bug for main. If the test is reading a removed field, update the test. Do not add retries. Retrying a deterministic failure only costs CI time.

**What the data shows.** It failed in 4 of 10 runs in CI with 4 workers, and passed 20 of 20 in isolation. The failure is a count mismatch, not a timeout. The combination of isolation stability and parallel instability is the signature of shared-state pollution.

**Root cause.** The test depends on the seeded tag named summer. tags.spec.ts renames that tag during its own run. With 4 workers the two specs sometimes overlap, and whichever runs second sees the other's state. The search test is the victim. tags.spec.ts is the offender. The expected count of 3 against a received 5 suggests the filter falls back to an unfiltered or broader list once the tag no longer matches. That detail is worth confirming when the fix is tested.

**Action.**

- Change tags.spec.ts so it creates its own tag with a unique name and renames that one. Seed data should be treated as read-only by every spec.

**Root cause.** The fixed sleep is a defect but it is not the direct cause. The assertion itself auto-waits for 5 seconds, so a 300 ms sleep cannot explain a 5 second timeout. Something prevents the total from ever reaching the expected value within 5 seconds in the failing runs. The two plausible explanations are:

- **The click is lost.** The button is visible before its handler is attached, so under 4-worker load the click lands before hydration and the total never changes.
- **The update is slow.** The cart recalculation takes more than 5 seconds under load, which would itself be a performance problem worth knowing about.

The failure message was summarised without the received text, so I cannot distinguish these. If the received value is the original total, the click was lost. If it is an intermediate value, the update is slow.

- If the click is being lost, wait for the button to be enabled or for a hydration marker before clicking. That is the actual fix for the lost-click case.

Only two of the four failing tests are flaky in the strict sense of "same code, non-deterministic result caused by the test or its environment". The other two are the suite doing its job. Treating all four as "flaky" and adding retries would hide one real regression and one real production bug.

## Per-test analysis

**profile > saves a new avatar. Not flaky.** It fails identically in all ten runs with the received value undefined. A 100% failure rate with a constant message is a deterministic defect, not flakiness, and no retry or quarantine policy applies. The undefined value means the property the test reads does not exist on the object it inspects. Two causes fit equally well, and the next step is the same for both: either the API or the page model renamed or dropped the avatar field, so the product regressed, or the test reads a field that was renamed on purpose, so the test is stale.

Assumption: this test passed on main before c0ffee1. Bisect from the last green run to find the commit. If the product regressed, revert or fix forward and keep the test unchanged. If the field was intentionally renamed, update the test and add the rename to the changelog of the same pull request. Until it is fixed, every CI run on main is red, which trains people to ignore CI and lets the genuinely flaky tests hide behind it. This is the first thing to do.

**search > filters results by tag. Flaky, caused by another spec.** The evidence is complete. It passes 20 of 20 when run alone in a single worker. It fails only in the parallel suite, and it fails when tags.spec.ts has already renamed the shared seeded tag "summer" on another worker. After the rename the filter no longer matches a real tag, the search falls back to an unfiltered list, and the test sees 5 results instead of 3. The failure rate of 40% is just the probability that tags.spec.ts gets scheduled before the search assertion under 4 workers.

The search test is the victim. The defect is in tags.spec.ts, which mutates shared seed data that other tests depend on. Fix it there:

- tags.spec.ts must create its own tag with a unique name, rename that, and delete it afterwards. It must never touch the seed.
- Treat seed data as read-only for the whole suite. Any test that needs to mutate an entity creates that entity itself, ideally through a fixture that generates a unique suffix per test and cleans up in teardown.
- Harden search.spec.ts the same way so it does not depend on the seed either. Creating its own three tagged items makes the expected count self-evident and removes the dependency entirely.

Do not fix this with serial mode or by pinning the two specs to the same worker. That hides the shared-state problem and slows the suite. Do not quarantine the search test; it will go green the moment tags.spec.ts stops mutating the seed.

**cart > updates the total when the quantity changes. Flaky, test-side, cause not yet proven.** The failure message is a retrying web-first assertion that waited the full five seconds and never saw the expected total. That matters because the fixed 300 ms sleep in the test is a smell but cannot be the cause of a five-second timeout; the assertion already retries far longer than the sleep. Something made the total never reach €58.00 at all, not merely reach it late.

Three candidate causes, in order of likelihood. The "+" button is clicked before the client-side handler is attached, so the click is swallowed and the quantity never changes; under four workers the browser and server are slower, hydration takes longer, and the race is lost about one time in three. Second, the cart belongs to a shared user and another spec running in parallel changes the cart contents, so the starting total differs and the expected value is wrong. Third, the cart update has the same read-after-write staleness seen in the orders test, so the page shows the old total after the update.

Assumption: the full report includes the received string. That one line decides it. If the received value is the original total, the click was lost or the update was stale. If it is a different non-starting value, the cart is shared and another test changed it. To confirm:

- Run it alone with `--repeat-each=50 --workers=1`. If it goes green alone, it is parallel interference and the fix is a unique user per test, as for search. If it still fails alone, it is a timing race inside the test or the app.
- Turn on trace retention on failure and look at whether the click produced a cart update request.
- Regardless of the result, delete the hard sleep, assert that the quantity control is enabled or hydrated before clicking, and assert the quantity field shows the new value before asserting the total. That turns one five-second timeout into a precise failure that names the step that broke.

Keep this test running. It is the only one of the four where the root cause is still open, so it goes on the flaky list with an owner and a deadline of one week to close out the investigation.

**orders > shows the latest order first. Not a flaky test; a real intermittent bug.** The team already did the right experiment. Alone, serial, with web-first assertions and a fresh user for every iteration, it still failed 3 of 50, and in those runs GET /orders omitted the order that was just created for up to two seconds. The test has no shared state, no fixed sleeps, and no parallel neighbours, and it still fails. Nothing on the test side remains to fix. The web-first assertion did not rescue it because the page fetches the list once on navigation; retrying the DOM assertion cannot refetch a stale list.

This is a read-after-write consistency gap. The most common sources are reads served from a replica that lags the primary, a response cache that is not invalidated on create, or an asynchronous indexing step. Real users hit exactly this: place an order, open the orders page, and the order is missing. The test caught a production defect.

Actions:

- File a backend bug with the 3-of-50 reproduction and the two-second window. Decide explicitly whether orders must be read-your-writes consistent. If yes, fix the read path, for example by reading from the primary after a write, invalidating the cache on create, or returning the created order in the response and having the page use it.
- Do not add a retry or poll to the test to make it green. That codifies the bug as acceptable behaviour with no one deciding so.
- If the product owner decides eventual consistency is acceptable, the product needs a visible pending state and the test should change to reflect the new spec: reload until the order appears within a bounded window and assert the pending state while waiting. That is a spec change, not a flake fix.
- Link the test to the bug ticket with an annotation. If it blocks merges while the bug is open, move it to a non-blocking quarantine project that still runs on every commit and reports, rather than skipping it. Reinstate it as blocking when the bug is fixed.

**login > signs in with valid credentials. Stable.** Ten of ten with no failures. Ten runs give only moderate confidence; a test with a 10% failure rate would pass all ten about a third of the time. No action is needed, but it should stay in the same ten-run rerun loop as the rest of the suite so that any later drift shows up.

## Suite-level actions

- **Fix profile first.** A permanently red main makes every other signal worthless. Nothing else in this list should wait for it, but it is the only item that is blocking today.
- **Keep retries at 0 on main.** Retries are what let the orders bug and the tags.spec.ts data mutation go undetected elsewhere. If merges need stability, retry only in the quarantine project and keep the blocking project strict.
- **Make seed data immutable and give every test its own data.** The search failure is one instance of a pattern that will recur. Add a fixture that creates a unique user and unique entities per test and tears them down. Audit the suite for other specs that mutate seeded rows.
- **Ban fixed sleeps.** Enable the Playwright ESLint rule that forbids waitForTimeout. It did not cause the cart failure, but it hides whatever did and it will cause others.
- **Retain traces on failure in CI.** The cart investigation is stalled only because there is no trace. One setting change fixes that for every future investigation.
- **Run a flakiness detector on every merge.** Run each changed spec ten times with repeat-each before it lands. Both flaky tests here would have been caught by that gate.
- **Separate the vocabulary.** "Flaky" should mean the test or its environment is wrong. Profile is a regression. Orders is a product bug. Calling all four flaky would have led to retries, and retries would have shipped the orders bug.

### profile > saves a new avatar (10/10 failed)

This is not flaky and must not be treated as flaky. Ten of ten identical failures on one commit is a deterministic defect. Received `undefined` where "avatar.png" was expected means the field the test reads no longer exists on the object it reads it from. That is either a product regression in c0ffee1 (avatar not persisted, or response shape changed) or a test that was never updated after an API or DOM change.

What to do:
1. Check whether c0ffee1 or its recent ancestors touched the profile or upload code. If yes, it is a regression and the commit should not ship.
2. If the product code did not change, the test's selector or field name is stale. Fix the test, but confirm manually that avatar save actually works first.
3. Do not add this to any flaky list, do not retry it, and do not quarantine it. A consistently failing test is a signal, not noise.

### search > filters results by tag (4/10 failed)

Root cause is confirmed: test interdependence through shared mutable state. The test expects 3 results tagged "summer". tags.spec.ts renames that tag during its own run. With 4 workers, whether search.spec.ts runs before, during, or after the rename depends on scheduling, which explains 4/10 in CI and 20/20 when run alone with one worker. "Expected 3, received 5" fits: once "summer" is gone the filter likely falls through to an unfiltered or default result set.

This is a test defect. The product is behaving correctly.

What to do:
1. Give each spec its own data. search.spec.ts should create a tag with a unique name (for example a UUID suffix) in `beforeEach`, tag its own fixtures, and delete them in `afterEach`.
2. tags.spec.ts should rename a tag it created itself, never a shared seed.
3. Add a lint or review rule: specs must not mutate seeded data. Mutation of shared seeds is the most common cause of worker-order flakes and this will recur elsewhere if it is not addressed as a policy.

Most likely cause (assumption, needs traces to confirm): the "+" click lands before the app has attached its handler, so the click is lost and the total never changes. Under 4 workers the runner is slower, hydration takes longer, and a 300 ms sleep is sometimes not enough. A second possibility is that the quantity update round-trip takes more than 5 s under load. A third is a genuine intermittent bug where the total does not recompute.

What to do:
1. Rerun this spec with `--repeat-each=50` under `--workers=4` and `trace: 'on'`. Look at the failing traces. If the click happened and no network request followed, it is a lost click. If a request went out and the response was slow, it is load. If the response came back and the DOM did not update, it is a product bug.
2. Remove `waitForTimeout(300)`. Replace it with a readiness condition: wait for the "+" button to be enabled, or wait for the specific response with `page.waitForResponse` after the click, then assert with `toHaveText`.
3. If the app ships a non-interactive button before hydration, that is a product defect too. Users can lose clicks in the same way. Raise it with the cart team.
4. Until the rewrite lands, tag it `@flaky` in a dedicated flaky project so it does not block merges, but keep running it so the rate is tracked.

### orders > shows the latest order first (2/10 failed)

The test is correct and the product is wrong. The team already did the right diagnostic: web-first assertions, a fresh user per run, and still 3 of 50 failures with evidence that GET /orders returned a stale list for up to 2 s after creation. That is read-after-write inconsistency in the backend, most likely a read replica, a cache, or an asynchronous index. The 2/10 CI rate matches the 6 percent standalone rate within noise.

1. File a backend bug with the repro (`--repeat-each=50`, response payloads showing the missing order, timing). Severity: at least P2, since it affects the post-checkout flow.
2. Quarantine the test with `test.fixme` referencing the ticket, so CI goes green without losing the test.
3. Do not wrap the assertion in `expect.poll` or `toPass` to make it pass. That would mask the bug and turn a signal into permanent noise. If the product owner decides eventual consistency is the accepted contract, then and only then change the test to poll, and document the accepted lag.
4. Once the backend fix ships, remove the quarantine and run `--repeat-each=100` before declaring it stable.

### login > signs in with valid credentials (0/10 failed)

Stable. No action. It is useful as a control: it confirms the runner and the auth backend were healthy in every run, which rules out a whole-suite infrastructure cause for the other failures.

**No common infrastructure cause.** The flaky failures cluster on different runs (cart on R2, R5, R9; search on R2, R4, R7, R10; orders on R3, R8). Only R2 shows two flakes together. If a slow runner were the cause, failures would pile up in the same runs. They do not. Each test has its own independent cause.

1. profile avatar: real failure, investigate today.
2. orders: file the backend bug and quarantine the test.
3. search: fix data isolation. Small change, removes 40 percent of noise.
4. cart: collect traces, then rewrite the waits.

1. Pull the Playwright trace for a failing run and check whether the quantity field changed. If quantity did not change, it is the lost click. If quantity changed but the total did not, it is the slow recalculation.

# The e2e suite fails on and off on commit c0ffee1

Three tests are flaky, one test is broken rather than flaky, and one is stable. Each needs a different fix.

## What the 10 runs show

| Test | Failed | Verdict | Do this |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| profile > saves a new avatar | 10 of 10 | Not flaky. It fails every time. | Treat as a red build. Fix today. |
| search > filters results by tag | 4 of 10 | Flaky. Another spec changes its data. | Give each spec its own tag. |
| cart > updates the total when the quantity changes | 3 of 10 | Flaky. The test races the page. | Replace the fixed wait. |
| orders > shows the latest order first | 2 of 10 | Flaky. The product lags its own writes. | File a bug, then poll in the test. |
| login > signs in with valid credentials | 0 of 10 | Stable. | Nothing. |

The other 115 tests are not listed. Assumption: they passed 10 of 10.

## profile > saves a new avatar fails every run

This test is not flaky. It fails 10 times out of 10 with the same message, so the cause is fixed, not random. The assertion reads a value that is `undefined`.

Assumption: commit c0ffee1 renamed the field or test ID the test reads, or avatar upload is broken at this commit. Either way, main is red on every run.

1. Run the test once with a trace and look at the page after the upload.
2. If the avatar is shown, update the selector or field name in the test.
3. If the avatar is not shown, treat it as a regression. Fix the code or revert the commit.

Do not add retries and do not quarantine this test. A test that fails every time is a signal, not noise.

## search > filters results by tag shares a tag with tags.spec.ts

The test filters by the seeded tag "summer". With 4 workers, tags.spec.ts sometimes renames that tag before search.spec.ts reads it, so the filter matches the wrong rows. Alone, the test passed 20 of 20, which confirms the cause is shared data, not the test logic.

1. In search.spec.ts, create a tag with a unique name in `beforeEach` and delete it in `afterEach`.
2. In tags.spec.ts, rename a tag the spec created itself, never a seeded one.
3. Run both specs together with `--workers=4 --repeat-each=20` and confirm 0 failures.

Do not fix this by setting `--workers=1` or by marking the specs serial. That hides the shared data and slows the whole suite.

## cart > updates the total when the quantity changes races the page

The test selects **+**, sleeps 300 ms, then waits up to 5 s for the total to read "€58.00". The assertion already waits, so the sleep is not the problem by itself. The total never reaches "€58.00" within 5 s, which means the click did not take effect.

Assumption: under 4 workers the page is slower, and the click lands before the page's script attaches the handler. The click is lost.

1. Remove `page.waitForTimeout(300)`.
2. Before the click, assert the state that proves the page is ready, for example that the total shows the price for 1 item. Assumption: that is "€29.00".
3. Select **+**.
4. Assert that the quantity reads 2, then that the total reads "€58.00".

If the test still fails, open the trace and check whether the click registered. If the app drops clicks before it is ready, users lose them too. That is an app bug, and the test should stay red until it is fixed.

## orders > shows the latest order first reads a stale list

This test failed 2 of 10 in CI and 3 of 50 alone, with web-first assertions and a new user each run. So test order and worker count are not the cause. In the failing runs, `GET /orders` returned the list without the new order for up to 2 s after it was created.

Assumption: the list reads from a replica or cache that lags the write. A user who places an order and opens the orders page within 2 s sees the same stale list.

1. File a bug against the orders API for read-after-write consistency. The product owner decides whether a 2 s lag is acceptable.
2. Until the bug is fixed, make the test wait for the list to include the new order with `expect.poll` or `toPass`, with a 5 s limit. Add a comment with the bug link.
3. When the bug is fixed, remove the poll and confirm 50 of 50 with `--repeat-each=50`.

Do not skip or quarantine this test. It found a real product gap.

## login > signs in with valid credentials is stable

It passed 10 of 10. Nothing to do. A sample of 10 shows the failure rate is low, not that it is zero.

## For the whole suite

- Keep `retries: 0` on main. A retry hides the search and orders failures.
- Set `trace: 'retain-on-failure'` so a failed run leaves a trace without a retry.
- Give every spec its own data. Shared seed data is the usual cause of failures that only appear with several workers.
- Count a test as fixed only after 0 failures in 20 runs with 4 workers on the fix commit.

## Before you re-run or ask for help, collect

- The run number and the worker that ran the failing test.
- The trace file for the failing test.
- The list of specs that ran on the same worker just before it.

- **+** is the quantity button in the cart.
- The total for 1 item in the cart test is "€29.00".
- `cart-total` is the test ID the test reads.

Of the 5 tests that failed in 10 runs of commit c0ffee1, 3 are flaky, 1 is broken on every run, and 1 is healthy.

| Test | Failed | Verdict | Cause | What to do |

| search > filters results by tag | 4 of 10 | Flaky | tags.spec.ts renames the seeded tag while this spec runs | Give tags.spec.ts its own tag |
| cart > updates the total when the quantity changes | 3 of 10 | Flaky | The click lands before the page is ready; a fixed wait hides it | Replace the fixed wait with a readiness check |
| orders > shows the latest order first | 2 of 10 | Flaky | The orders API returns a stale list for up to 2 s | Raise a backend bug; reload until the order appears |
| login > signs in with valid credentials | 0 of 10 | Healthy | None | None |

The sections below are in order of how often each test fails.

## profile > saves a new avatar fails on every run

A test that fails 10 of 10 times with the same message is not flaky. It is broken. The received value is undefined, so the test reads a property that the page or the save response no longer has. Either the product stopped returning the file name after a save, or the field was renamed and the test was not updated.

1. Treat this as a red build on main, not as a flaky test. Do not add a retry and do not skip it.
2. Run the spec alone with tracing on and check what the save request returns.
3. If the product no longer returns the file name, fix the product. If the field was renamed, update the test.
4. If the test also fails on earlier commits, find the first failing commit with `git bisect`.

## search > filters results by tag fails when tags.spec.ts runs at the same time

This test passes 20 of 20 times alone with 1 worker and fails 4 of 10 times in the suite. That pattern means another test changes shared data. Both specs use the same seeded database, and with 4 workers the two files run side by side in a different order each run. When tags.spec.ts renames the "summer" tag first, the filter finds no tag with that name and the page shows all 5 unfiltered results.

1. Change tags.spec.ts so it creates its own tag and renames that one. It must never change seeded data.
2. Optionally, have search.spec.ts create its own tag with a unique suffix and tag 3 items with it, so the test owns everything it reads.
3. Do not fix this by dropping to 1 worker or by restoring the name in an afterEach hook. Restoring still leaves a window where both specs overlap.
4. Confirm the fix with the full suite at 4 workers, repeated 10 times.

## cart > updates the total when the quantity changes times out

The assertion is already web-first and waits up to 5 s, so the fixed 300 ms wait is not what causes the timeout. It only hides the real problem. In the failing runs the total never reaches €58.00 within 5 s of the click, which means the click was lost or the update stalled. The most likely reason is that the "+" control is visible before the page has attached its handler, so Playwright clicks too early. Load from 4 workers widens that window.

1. Remove `page.waitForTimeout(300)`.
2. Before clicking "+", wait for a signal that the page is interactive. If the app has no such signal, add one, for example a disabled state on the quantity control until the page is ready, or a data attribute set after hydration.
3. Keep the web-first assertion on the total.
4. Run the spec with `--repeat-each=50 --workers=4` and check the trace of any remaining failure. If the trace shows the click registered and the total still stalled, the cause is a slow price update, and the fix moves to the product.

## orders > shows the latest order first shows the previous order

This test still fails 3 of 50 times alone, with a new user per run and web-first assertions, so neither test interference nor the assertion style is the cause. The orders API returns the list without the new order for up to 2 s after the order is created. That is read-after-write lag in the backend, most likely a cache or a read replica. A web-first assertion cannot help, because the page fetches the list once on load and the DOM never changes.

This is a product behaviour as well as a test problem. A customer who places an order and opens their orders page can see the old list for 2 s.

1. Raise a backend issue for the stale read and decide with the product owner whether a 2 s delay is acceptable.
2. Until the backend is fixed, make the test reload the page until the order appears, with a bounded timeout:

```ts
await expect(async () => {
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-row').first()).toHaveText('Order #1043');
}).toPass({ timeout: 10_000 });
```

3. Do not widen a fixed timeout instead. It makes every run slower and still fails when the lag is longer.
4. When the backend is fixed, remove the reload loop and return to a plain assertion.

## login > signs in with valid credentials is healthy

This test passed 10 of 10 times. No action is needed.

## While you fix them

- Keep the 3 flaky tests running. Tag them so the team can track them, and fix them within the sprint. Skipping them hides regressions in cart, search and orders.
- Set `retries: 1` with `trace: 'on-first-retry'` on main so each flake leaves a trace. Playwright reports a pass on retry as flaky, not as passed, so the count stays visible.
- Before closing any of the 4 tickets, run the spec with `--repeat-each=50 --workers=4`. This reproduces the suite conditions better than a run with 1 worker.

## Assumptions

- All 10 runs used the same seeded database, shared by all 4 workers.
- The differences between runs come from worker scheduling and machine load, not from code or infrastructure changes.
- The other 115 tests passed in all 10 runs.
- The cart page renders the "+" control before its handler is attached.
- The search page shows the unfiltered list when the requested tag does not exist.
- The avatar test fails the same way on every machine, not only in CI.

Fix the spec that changes shared data, not the spec that reads it.

1. In tags.spec.ts, create a new tag in `beforeEach` and rename that tag instead of "summer".
2. Check tags.spec.ts for any other seed row it changes or deletes, and give each one its own created row.
3. Add a rule to the suite README: a spec may read seed data, but it must create any data it changes.

2. In `tags.spec.ts`, do the same instead of renaming the seeded tag.
3. Delete both tags in `afterEach`.

Do not move the two specs to a serial project. That hides the problem and slows the suite.

## cart: the test waits a fixed 300 ms instead of waiting for the page

The test selects **+** and then waits 300 ms with `page.waitForTimeout(300)`. The 5000 ms assertion timeout on `cart-total` then expires, so the total never became €58.00 at all. A fixed wait cannot cause that on its own, so the click itself is lost on slow runs.

Assumption: on a loaded runner the page has rendered **+** before its handler is attached, so the click does nothing and the total stays unchanged.

Fix: wait for a condition, not for time.

1. Remove `page.waitForTimeout(300)`.
2. Before selecting **+**, wait for the quantity field to show its starting value with `expect(quantity).toHaveValue('1')`.
3. Select **+** and wait for the cart request with `page.waitForResponse` on the cart endpoint.
4. Keep the `toHaveText('€58.00')` assertion as it is.

If the test still fails after this change, the lost click is a product bug and needs a ticket with a trace.

This is the only case where the product causes the flake. Run alone, with web-first assertions and a new user every time, the spec failed 3 of 50. In those runs the orders list did not include the order just created for up to 2 seconds.

Assumption: the list is served from a cache or a read replica that lags behind writes.

Fix in the test now:

1. Wrap the check in `expect(async () => { await page.reload(); await expect(firstRow).toHaveText('Order #1043'); }).toPass({ timeout: 5000 })`.
2. Keep the timeout at 5 seconds so a real regression still fails quickly.

This test failed 10 of 10 and is not flaky. It expects `avatar.png` and receives `undefined`, so the value it reads is missing, not wrong. A test that always fails on main should block merges until it is fixed.

Assumption: the response or page object no longer has the property the test reads, because the avatar save changed shape or was never finished on this commit.

Fix today:

1. Run the test alone with a trace and check where `undefined` comes from.
2. If the product no longer returns the field, fix the product or update the test to the new field name.
3. Do not mark this test as flaky and do not add retries to it.

## login: stable

This test passed 10 of 10. No action.

- Keep retries at 0 on main so flakes stay visible.
- Do not quarantine any of the 3 flaky tests. Each has a known fix that takes under an hour.
- Collect a Playwright trace for any new failure before re-running, so the team is not guessing from a message alone.

Assumption: the other 115 tests passed in all 10 runs and need no action.

## Updates

- None: first version.

# e2e suite fails on main with no code change

If the e2e suite fails on a commit that already passed, 3 tests are flaky, 1 test is broken on every run, and the rest are stable.

This analysis covers 10 runs of commit c0ffee1 on main, with Playwright, 4 workers and retries set to 0. Assumption: the 115 tests not listed in the report passed in all 10 runs.

| Test | Failed | Verdict | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| profile > saves a new avatar | 10 of 10 | Broken, not flaky | Fix the regression |
| search > filters results by tag | 4 of 10 | Flaky: shared test data | Give each spec its own tag |
| cart > updates the total when the quantity changes | 3 of 10 | Flaky: fixed sleep before the click | Wait for the control, then assert |
| orders > shows the latest order first | 2 of 10 | Flaky: API returns stale data | File a product bug, poll in the test for now |
| login > signs in with valid credentials | 0 of 10 | Stable | None |

With 3 independent flaky tests at these rates, a run is fully green about 1 time in 3. The profile test alone made every one of the 10 runs red.

## profile > saves a new avatar fails every run

The test expects "avatar.png" and receives undefined in all 10 runs. A test that fails the same way every time is not flaky. Something on main returns no file name, in the app or in the test.

Assumption: a recent commit changed the field the test reads, and the test was not updated.

1. Find the last commit where this test passed, with `git bisect` or the CI history.
2. Fix the app if users lose the avatar name, or fix the test if only the field name changed.
3. Do not quarantine this test. It reports a real failure on main.

## search > filters results by tag fails with other specs running

The test passes 20 of 20 alone and fails 4 of 10 with 4 workers. It filters by the seeded tag "summer", and tags.spec.ts renames that tag during its own run. When the two specs overlap, the search finds 5 results instead of 3.

The cause is shared test data, not timing. Running with 1 worker would hide it and slow the suite.

1. In search.spec.ts, create a tag with a unique name in `beforeEach` and search for that tag.
2. In tags.spec.ts, rename a tag the spec creates itself, not a seeded one.
3. Search the suite for other specs that change seeded data and apply the same rule.

## cart > updates the total when the quantity changes times out

The test selects **+**, waits a fixed 300 ms, and then waits up to 5 s for the total to read "€58.00". The 5 s wait is already a web-first assertion, so the total never changed. The most likely reason is that the select lands before the page has attached its handlers, so the increment is lost.

Assumption: the page hydrates after load and the **+** control is visible before it works.

1. Remove the `page.waitForTimeout(300)` call.
2. Before the select, assert the starting total, for example `await expect(total).toHaveText("€29.00")`.
3. Assert that **+** is enabled, then select it.
4. Keep the `toHaveText("€58.00")` assertion as the only wait after the select.

If the test still fails after this change, record a trace with `--trace on` and check whether the select reached the handler.

## orders > shows the latest order first shows the previous order

The test creates an order, opens the list and expects "Order #1043" first. In 2 of 10 CI runs and 3 of 50 isolated runs, GET /orders returned the list without the new order for up to 2 s after creation. The test already uses web-first assertions and a fresh user, so the test is not the cause.

This is a product behaviour. A user who places an order and opens their orders page can see the same stale list.

1. File a bug against the orders API. Include the request IDs and the 2 s delay from the repeat run.
2. Until the API is fixed, poll GET /orders with `expect.poll` until the new order appears, then open the page.
3. Add a comment linking the bug so the poll is removed when the API is fixed.

Assumption: the delay comes from a read replica or a cache. The backend team can confirm.

## login > signs in with valid credentials

Stable in 10 of 10 runs. No action.

## Keep retries at 0 until these are fixed

Turning on retries would hide the 3 flaky tests and the broken profile test behind a green badge. Keep retries at 0 until the 4 fixes above land, then consider `retries: 1` on CI only, with the flaky status reported on the run.

## Before you mark any other test as flaky

Collect these before changing the test:

- The run IDs where it failed and passed on the same commit.
- The result of `npx playwright test <spec> --workers=1 --repeat-each=20`.
- The failure message, to check it is the same on every failure.

A test that fails alone with the same message every time is broken, not flaky.

## Labels assumed

- The quantity control in the cart is labelled **+**.
- The cart total uses the test id `cart-total`.
- Order titles appear as "Order #1043".

# Flaky test analysis: e2e suite at c0ffee1 (main)

**Source:** 10 CI runs of the same commit, Playwright, 4 workers, `retries: 0`, 120 tests. Read only: the run table and the failure messages supplied. Nothing was run by me; the repeat runs quoted below are the team's own, as reported.

**Assumptions (information not supplied):**
- The 115 tests not in the table passed in all 10 runs. If any of them has a mixed record, it is a suspect too and belongs in the ledger.
- Quarantine period and escalation threshold: the `testing-guidelines` rule could not be loaded (see the end of this report), so I use **one sprint = 2 weeks** (deadline 2026-11-09 from today, 2026-10-26) and treat **more than 5% of the suite quarantined** as the escalation point. Replace both with the rule's values.
- Test IDs are `<spec file> > <title>`; owners are "TBD" until the team assigns them. A row without an owner is not yet a quarantine.

## 1. Verdict per test

| Test | Failures / runs | Verdict | Cause class |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cart > updates the total when the quantity changes | 3 / 10 | **Flaky** | Test timing (provisional, see below) |
| profile > saves a new avatar | 10 / 10 | **Deterministic failure, not flaky** | Defect (product or test), main is red |
| search > filters results by tag | 4 / 10 | **Flaky** | Order or shared state (cross-spec data mutation) |
| orders > shows the latest order first | 2 / 10 | **Flaky** | **Product intermittent defect** (eventual consistency) |
| login > signs in with valid credentials | 0 / 10 | Not a suspect | 0 failures in 10 runs; this bounds the rate, it does not prove zero |

## 2. Why, and what to do with each

### cart > updates the total when the quantity changes: fix the test, then re-check

**Evidence.** Fails 3 of 10 with `Timeout 5000ms exceeded waiting for getByTestId('cart-total') to have text "€58.00"`. The test clicks "+" and then calls `page.waitForTimeout(300)` before asserting.

**Reading.** The hard sleep is a `code-style-qa` violation and must go, but note what the message says: the final assertion is already web-first and waited a further 5 s. So the sleep is not what fails; something after the click takes longer than 5.3 s, or the click never registered (clicked before the handler was attached, a common cause when the test clicks right after navigation). Under 4 workers the app is also under load, which widens the window.

**Classification:** test timing, provisional. What decides it: open the Playwright trace of one failed run and check whether the quantity changed and whether the cart update request was sent. If the request was sent and the response carried the new total but the DOM did not update, this is a product defect and moves to `/qa-defect`.

**Fix.** Remove the sleep. Wait for the cart update response (`page.waitForResponse` on the cart endpoint, started before the click) and assert the quantity field first, then the total, with `expect(...).toHaveText(...)`. Do not raise the assertion timeout as the fix.

**Exit proof.** On the fix commit: `npx playwright test cart.spec.ts --workers=4 --repeat-each=50` with 0 failures recorded, plus red-green: break the total calculation (or stub the response with the old total) and confirm the test fails.

### profile > saves a new avatar: not flaky, report it now

**Evidence.** Fails 10 of 10 with `Expected: "avatar.png", Received: undefined`. Same message every run, no variance.

**Reading.** This is a deterministic failure on main. It is either a product defect (the saved avatar is not returned or not persisted) or a test defect (the test reads a property that no longer exists in the response or page). Either way, main has been red for 10 runs on this test and that is the first thing to say to the team. Per ISTQB CTFL §1.2.3 the cause may be a defect or the environment; one manual or API check settles which: save an avatar by hand and read the profile back.

**Action.** Do not quarantine; quarantine is for tests whose verdict changes. File it with `/qa-defect` as a reproducible defect ("Always", 10 of 10), assign an owner, and fix or revert the change that broke it. If the team must unblock the pipeline before the fix, skip it with the defect reference in the skip reason, not with `@quarantine`.

### search > filters results by tag: fix the data isolation

**Evidence.** Fails 4 of 10 in CI with `expected 3 results, received 5`. Alone (`npx playwright test search.spec.ts --workers=1 --repeat-each=20`) it passed 20 of 20. It filters by the seeded tag `summer`, which `tags.spec.ts` renames during its own run.

**Reading.** Textbook shared-state collision: with 4 workers, whether `tags.spec.ts` has already renamed `summer` when `search.spec.ts` queries it depends on scheduling. The 20 of 20 pass alone and the known mutation make the class certain.

**One thing to look at.** A renamed tag should give 0 results, not 5. If 5 is the unfiltered total, the search endpoint may be silently ignoring an unknown tag and returning everything. That is a product behaviour worth a quick check and possibly its own report; it is not what makes the test flaky.

**Fix.** Neither spec may use the shared seed `summer`. Each test creates its own tag with a unique name (for example suffixed with the test ID or a timestamp) in a `beforeEach` or fixture and cleans it up; `tags.spec.ts` renames only a tag it created. Do not fix it with serial mode or a fixed spec order; that hides the coupling and slows the suite.

**Exit proof.** On the fix commit: `npx playwright test --workers=4 --repeat-each=20 search.spec.ts tags.spec.ts` with 0 failures recorded, plus red-green: break the tag filter (return all results) and confirm the search test fails.

### orders > shows the latest order first: product defect, report with frequency

**Evidence.** Fails 2 of 10 in CI with `Expected "Order #1043", Received "Order #1042"`. The team's `--repeat-each=50` run of this spec alone, with web-first assertions and a fresh user per run, still failed 3 of 50. In those runs `GET /orders` returned the list without the new order for up to 2 s after creation.

**Reading.** Correct waits, isolated data, still fails, and the API itself is observed returning stale data. This is not a test problem. It is an intermittent product defect: an order exists but is not yet visible on read (read replica lag, a cache, or an asynchronous write). Quarantining it alone would hide a defect that real users will hit.

**Action.** File with `/qa-defect` as a **product** defect with the observed frequency: 3 of 50 alone, 2 of 10 in CI, stale read for up to 2 s. Quarantine the test with the report ID so the pipeline is not blocked, and keep it running in the non-blocking quarantine job so the product fix is visible when it lands. Do not fix the test by polling until the order appears or by adding a sleep; a test that waits out the staleness turns the defect into a pass.

**Exit proof.** After the product fix: `npx playwright test orders.spec.ts --workers=4 --repeat-each=100` with 0 failures recorded (the 3 of 50 base rate needs more than 50 runs to be meaningful), plus red-green: break the ordering and confirm the test fails.

### login > signs in with valid credentials

0 failures in 10 runs. No action. The sample is small; this bounds the failure rate, it does not prove the test is stable.

## 3. Quarantine proposal and ledger

Proposed rows for `flaky/ledger.md`. The team decides and assigns owners; nothing is quarantined until it does.

| Test ID | Cause class | Defect report | Owner | Quarantined on | Deadline | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cart.spec.ts > updates the total when the quantity changes | Test timing (provisional, confirm from trace) | None needed unless trace shows a product cause | TBD | 2026-10-26 | 2026-11-09 | quarantined |
| search.spec.ts > filters results by tag | Order or shared state (seed tag mutated by tags.spec.ts) | None (test-side); optional report for unknown-tag filter behaviour | TBD | 2026-10-26 | 2026-11-09 | quarantined |
| orders.spec.ts > shows the latest order first | Product intermittent defect (stale GET /orders up to 2 s) | DR to be filed via `/qa-defect`, frequency 3/50 alone, 2/10 in CI | TBD (product team) | 2026-10-26 | 2026-11-09 | quarantined |

Not in the ledger: `profile.spec.ts > saves a new avatar` (deterministic, defect report instead) and `login.spec.ts` (no evidence of flakiness).

**Share.** 3 quarantined of 120 listed tests = 2.5%. Under the assumed 5% threshold, so no escalation. Confirm the denominator with `npx playwright test --list` rather than the figure in the run summary.

**Pipeline changes.**
- Add `--grep-invert @quarantine` to the `@smoke` and `@regression` jobs.
- Add a separate, non-blocking job running `--grep @quarantine` on every pipeline run so fixes become visible.
- Keep `retries: 0`. Raising retries would make cart and search go green while leaving the causes in place, and would hide the orders defect entirely (ISTQB CTFL §6.2: relying on a tool without critical thinking).
- No self-healing selectors anywhere in the fix.

**At the deadline.** Each row is either retired (fixed, with the repeat-run output and red-green proof recorded) or deleted with the reason in the ledger, or extended with a recorded decision and a new date. Cart and search are small test-side fixes and should not need the full period.

## 4. What this history cannot show

- Runs before these 10 and on earlier commits; whether these tests were already flaky before c0ffee1.
- The other 115 tests; assumed stable at 10 of 10.
- Whether the CI environment itself was stable across the 10 runs (runner load, database latency). The stale read in orders may have an infrastructure component that only the service owner can see.
- Whether the cart click registered in the failed runs; the trace decides that.
- Why search received 5 results rather than 0; one manual query decides that.

**Rules not applied.** The `testing-guidelines` rule (quarantine period, escalation threshold and who to escalate to) and the `code-style-qa` rule could not be loaded: no `qa-rules` skill is installed and file lookup in the skill tree was denied in this session. The 2-week deadline and 5% threshold above are stated assumptions, not the rule's figures.
